results.summary: McDonald 2017 criteria require dissemination in space (DIS) across periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord regions, and dissemination in time (DIT) demonstrated by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, a new lesion on follow-up, or CSF oligoclonal bands. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is a classic infratentorial brainstem syndrome that counts toward DIS. Spinal cord lesions count toward DIS regardless of length, though NMOSD must be excluded.

results.summary: Short-segment spinal cord lesions (less than 3 vertebral segments, typically eccentric and dorsal) are characteristic of MS. results.title: Multiple sclerosis

output.summary: The McDonald 2017 criteria enable diagnosis of RRMS when dissemination in space and time are established by clinical and paraclinical means. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is a recognized brainstem presentation counting toward DIS. Short-segment eccentric cord lesions favor MS over NMOSD, in which longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM, ≥3 vertebral segments) is the characteristic spinal cord phenotype. CSF oligoclonal bands, when positive, can satisfy DIT in the appropriate clinical context. DMT choice requires JC virus serostatus assessment (for natalizumab), hepatitis B screening (for ocrelizumab/ofatumumab), and individualization based on disease activity, MRI burden, and patient reproductive and safety considerations.

alternatives: Ocrelizumab 600 mg IV every 6 months (anti-CD20, high efficacy, no JCV risk)
Dimethyl fumarate 240 mg PO BID (oral moderate efficacy, monitor lymphocytes)
Cladribine 3.5 mg/kg total over 2 years (oral immune reconstitution, requires lymphocyte monitoring)
contraindications: Natalizumab: contraindicated in JC virus antibody-positive patients at high PML risk (index >1.5 in previously natalizumab-treated patients, or any positivity in high-immunosuppression exposure); TOUCH program enrollment required
Ocrelizumab/ofatumumab: contraindicated in active hepatitis B infection — hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody must be screened prior to initiation
Active systemic infections or immunocompromising conditions are general contraindications to all immunomodulatory DMTs
output.formulary_status: Natalizumab and ocrelizumab formulary approved with prior authorization for confirmed RRMS diagnosis
interactions: Cetirizine: no clinically significant interaction with natalizumab or anti-CD20 DMTs.
Vitamin D3: no interaction; vitamin D supplementation is encouraged alongside DMT in MS.
output.proposed: Natalizumab 300 mg IV every 4 weeks (or alternative anti-CD20 agent)
warnings: Natalizumab: obtain JC virus antibody index at baseline and every 6 months; stratify PML risk by index and prior immunosuppressant use
Ocrelizumab 300 mg IV x2 (2 weeks apart), then 600 mg every 6 months: pre-medicate with methylprednisolone, antihistamine, antipyretic; monitor IgG levels; B-cell depletion expected
Live-attenuated vaccines are contraindicated after initiation of B-cell depleting agents or S1P modulators; ensure vaccination is up to date before starting
Fingolimod requires baseline ECG and first-dose monitoring for bradyarrhythmia; contraindicated in QTc prolongation or second-degree AV block
Teriflunomide is teratogenic with a long half-life; effective contraception required during treatment and accelerated elimination procedure needed after stopping if pregnancy desired
Sulfonamide allergy noted: teriflunomide has no sulfonamide cross-reactivity; no specific adjustment required for cetirizine or vitamin D

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose NMOSD based on a short eccentric cervical cord lesion spanning one segment — NMOSD requires LETM (≥3 contiguous vertebral segments) or AQP4-IgG positivity per 2015 international consensus criteria; a short MS-pattern cord lesion does not meet NMOSD criteria
Do not exclude NMOSD or MOGAD on clinical grounds alone — AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays are mandatory before initiating MS-specific DMT

Do not start natalizumab without obtaining JC virus antibody index and enrolling in the TOUCH prescribing program; PML risk is unacceptably high in JCV-positive patients with prior immunosuppressant exposure
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and mandatory first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring for at least 6 hours
Do not use ELISA-based AQP4 assays — cell-based assays (CBA) are required due to the unacceptable false-negative rate of ELISA
required_recommendations: Recognize left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) — failure of left eye adduction on rightward gaze with abducting nystagmus in the right eye — as indicating a left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) lesion, a classic and highly specific MS brainstem sign
Establish dissemination in space (DIS) across MS-typical regions: periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial (left pontine MLF), and spinal cord (C5-C6)
Establish dissemination in time (DIT) by demonstrating simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same MRI, confirmed additionally by CSF oligoclonal bands
Order AQP4-IgG (cell-based assay) and MOG-IgG (cell-based assay) to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD before committing to MS diagnosis and disease-modifying therapy

Characterize the cord lesion on dedicated spine MRI to confirm it is short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies) and eccentric — not longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM ≥3 segments), which would strongly favor NMOSD
Treat the acute relapse with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days); reserve plasma exchange for steroid-refractory severe disability

Initiate disease-modifying therapy after relapse stabilization; obtain JC virus antibody index before considering natalizumab; screen hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody before starting ocrelizumab or ofatumumab

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis — findings are non-specific and do not contribute to dissemination in space or time assessment.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for detecting demyelinating plaques and adds radiation without clinical benefit in this context.
No cardiac indication in a standard MS diagnostic workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac Holter monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation (bradyarrhythmia monitoring) — not as a diagnostic step for MS.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis and does not differentiate demyelinating disease from its mimics; adds substantial cost.

differential.key_features: Must be actively excluded — AQP4-IgG and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM, ≥3 vertebral segments) are the hallmarks; here AQP4-IgG negative and cord lesion is short (<2 segments)

Single clinical attack is the prior history at 18 months; current episode plus background prior attack, DIS, DIT, and positive OCBs satisfy McDonald 2017 for full RRMS diagnosis rather than CIS alone
Can produce periventricular and brainstem lesions; typically also leptomeningeal/pachymeningeal enhancement, elevated serum ACE, lymphopenia, hilar adenopathy — absent here
Subacute combined degeneration causes symmetric dorsal column myelopathy; B12 normal at 392 pg/mL, no macrocytic anemia, and brainstem/periventricular brain lesions not explained by B12 deficiency
Could explain myelopathic signs at C5-C6 level; however MRI shows no disc herniation or cord compression, and brain periventricular/brainstem lesions are not explained by cervical spondylosis

key_clinical_evidence: Left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (left eye fails to adduct, right eye abducts with nystagmus on rightward gaze) localizes to the left MLF in the dorsal pons — a classic, high-specificity demyelinating brainstem sign that counts toward infratentorial DIS under the 2024 revised McDonald

The cervical cord lesion (C5-C6, one segment, eccentric right-lateral) is short and asymmetric — the pattern characteristic of MS; NMOSD characteristically causes longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM: ≥3 contiguous segments, often central) — the most important red herring for this case

DIS is established across four MS-typical regions: periventricular (multiple), juxtacortical (left frontal), infratentorial (left dorsal pons/MLF), and spinal cord (C5-C6) — the 2024 revised McDonald requires at least two
DIT is satisfied doubly: simultaneous gadolinium-enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the index MRI, and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (4 bands, absent in paired serum)

AQP4-IgG negative by cell-based assay effectively excludes seropositive NMOSD; MOG-IgG negative excludes MOGAD — both required because partial cord myelopathy is the presenting cord phenotype of all three conditions

Mild left optic disc pallor on fundoscopy with no historical optic neuritis — confirmed by OCT (RNFL/GCL thinning left > right) and VEP (prolonged left P100 latency) — represents a prior subclinical optic pathway demyelinating event contributing evidence of dissemination in space and time

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

July 2026 review applied end to end: brain and cervical/thoracic cord MRI use an MS protocol; CSF is conditional, never mandatory; OCT/VEP and AQP4/MOG testing answer selected optic or atypical questions rather than forming a blanket panel.

The 2024 revised McDonald framework recognizes the optic nerve as a fifth topography and accepts the kappa free-light-chain index as an alternative positive-CSF marker; these additions do not make optic testing or lumbar puncture universal.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Daniel Rowe is a 34-year-old right-handed man admitted to the neurology service with a 12-day history of progressively worsening right leg weakness and a 9-day history of horizontal double vision. He first noticed difficulty initiating the right leg swing while cycling to work, with the right leg feeling heavy and uncoordinated. Over the following days, the weakness progressed such that he began dragging the right foot when fatigued, and he abandoned cycling four days ago due to fear of falling. He also reports a new band of numbness and reduced sensation over the right leg from mid-thigh to the foot, onset approximately 10 days ago, and urinary urgency over the past week with two near-incontinence episodes. Nine days ago, he developed horizontal diplopia, which he initially dismissed as fatigue. He noticed that it occurred specifically when looking to the right and that the images were separated horizontally. He has not had any eye pain, no loss of visual acuity, and no color desaturation. On further questioning he recalls an episode 18 months ago of left leg numbness and tingling from the knee downward that lasted approximately 4 weeks and then resolved completely. He was told by his primary care physician that this was likely a herniated lumbar disc; no MRI or further evaluation was performed. He also notes that on looking back, his right leg symptoms transiently worsen after hot showers. He denies any fever, night sweats, weight loss, headache, nausea, oral ulcers, joint pains, rash, or sick contacts. He has not traveled recently. His paternal uncle was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis at age 41.
